Hagah
haw-GAW
verb
Hebrew hagah, “to murmur, mutter, moan, meditate”; the word for the low utterance of one pondering the law of God.

📖 Biblical Definition

Hagah is the Hebrew verb that lies behind the biblical word meditate, and it means far more than silent thought: it is to murmur, to mutter, to ponder aloud in a low voice, the sound of a man turning God’s Word over and over upon his tongue and in his heart. The blessed man of the first Psalm is the one whose delight is in the law of the LORD, and in His law doth he meditate—hagah—day and night; like a tree planted by the rivers of water, he brings forth his fruit in his season. Joshua was charged to let the book of the law not depart out of his mouth but to meditate therein day and night. The psalmist meditates upon God in the night watches, remembers the days of old and muses on the works of His hands. Biblical meditation is thus the opposite of the emptied mind sought in Eastern and modern practice: it is the filling of the mind with the Word of God, the deliberate, repeated, even murmured chewing of Scripture until it nourishes the soul. The dictionary reads hagah as the appointed exercise of godliness—not vacancy but occupation, not emptying but filling—the believer’s low and constant muttering over the law of his God, the secret of the fruitful and prosperous life.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Hebrew verb behind “meditate”—to murmur, mutter, ponder aloud; the filling of the mind with God’s Word, the opposite of the emptied mind of false meditation.

expand to see more

HAGAH, Hebrew “to murmur, mutter, meditate” on the Word of God.

More than silent thought: pondering Scripture aloud, turning it over and over.

The blessed man meditates in the law of the LORD day and night (Psa 1:2).

Biblical meditation fills the mind; it does not empty it.

The secret of the fruitful and prosperous life.

📖 Key Scripture

Psa 1:2 — "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night."

Psa 63:6 — "When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches."

Psa 143:5 — "I remember the days of old; I meditate on all thy works; I muse on the work of thy hands."

Psa 77:12 — "I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Eastern and modern “meditation” seeks to empty the mind and merge with the divine; biblical hagah fills the mind with God’s Word and fixes it upon His works.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the wholesale replacement of biblical meditation by its Eastern and modern counterfeit. The mindfulness and transcendental practices flooding the West aim to empty the mind, to detach from thought, to dissolve the self into an impersonal divine—the very opposite of hagah. Where the world’s meditation seeks vacancy, Scripture’s seeks occupation; where the one empties, the other fills; where the one merges the self into the All, the other fixes the soul upon the personal God and His revealed Word. To borrow the methods of the emptied mind under the name of meditation is to take a poison for a medicine.

The principle to recover is meditation as the filling of the mind with the Word of God. Hagah is the low, constant murmuring of Scripture, the turning of the law of the LORD over and over until it lodges in the heart; the blessed man does it day and night and is fruitful as a watered tree. The believer meditates on God upon his bed, muses on the works of His hands, talks of His doings—not emptying himself into silence but feeding his soul on the truth. This is the appointed exercise of godliness, and the spring of a prosperous and fruitful walk.
